question: Within how many days must a resident policyholder repatriate the maturity proceeds or claim amount of a life insurance policy issued by an insurer outside India, if the premium was paid via remittance from India?
answer: Within a period of seven days from the receipt of the proceeds or claim.
supporting_quote: If the premium due on a life insurance policy has been paid by making remittance from India, the policy holder shall repatriate to India through normal banking channels, the maturity proceeds or amount of any claim due on the policy, within a period of seven days from the receipt thereof.

question: If a resident of Nepal or Bhutan receives a claim payment in a foreign currency under a general or health insurance policy from an Indian insurer, under what condition is prior approval from the Reserve Bank of India NOT required?
answer: Prior approval is not required if the premium on the policy was also collected in foreign currency.
supporting_quote: Payments in foreign currency towards claims under general/health insurance policies will require prior approval of Reserve Bank, except where premium thereon was also collected in foreign currency.

question: How do the settlement rules for claims on rupee life insurance policies differ between foreign nationals who are not permanently resident in India and Indians resident outside India who paid premiums in non-repatriable rupees?
answer: For foreign nationals not permanently resident in India, claims or maturity proceeds may be paid in rupees or allowed to be remitted abroad. In contrast, for Indians resident outside India whose premiums were collected in non-repatriable rupees, payments may only be paid in rupees by credit to their NRO account.
supporting_quote: Claims/maturity proceeds/ surrender value in respect of rupee life insurance policies issued to Indians resident outside India for which premium have been collected in non-repatriable rupees may be paid only in rupees by credit to NRO account of the beneficiary. ... Claims/maturity proceeds/ surrender value in respect of rupee policies issued to foreign nationals not permanently resident in India may be paid in rupees or may be allowed to be remitted abroad, if the claimant so desires.

question: Under what definition is a person considered "not permanently resident" in India for the purpose of foreign exchange regulations relating to life insurance?
answer: A person resident in India for employment of a specified duration (regardless of length) or for a specific job or assignment, where the duration does not exceed three years.
supporting_quote: ‘Not permanently resident' means a person resident in India for employment of a specified duration (irrespective of length thereof) or for a specific job or assignment, the duration of which does not exceed three years.

question: What are the differences in the required profit-making track record and minimum net worth between a foreign entity establishing a Branch Office (BO) and one establishing a Liaison Office (LO) in India?
answer: A Branch Office requires a profit-making track record during the immediately preceding five financial years in its home country and a net worth of at least USD 100,000. In contrast, a Liaison Office requires a profit-making track record during the immediately preceding three financial years and a net worth of at least USD 50,000.
supporting_quote:
For Branch Office — a profit making track record during the immediately preceding five financial years in the home country and net worth of not less than USD 100,000 or its equivalent.

Net Worth [total of paid-up capital and free reserves, less intangible assets as per the latest Audited Balance Sheet or Account Statement certified by a Certified Public Accountant or any Registered Accounts Practitioner by whatever name called].

b. For Liaison Office — a profit making track record during the immediately preceding three financial years in the home country and net worth of not less than USD 50,000 or its equivalent.

question: Within what time frame must a foreign entity open its BO/LO/PO after receiving approval before the approval lapses, and what is the maximum extension the AD Category-I bank can grant?
answer: The BO/LO/PO must be opened within six months from the date of the approval letter, otherwise the approval lapses. If the entity cannot open the office within this timeframe due to reasons beyond its control, the AD Category-I bank may grant an extension of up to an additional six months.
supporting_quote: The approval granted by the AD Category I bank should include a proviso to the effect that in case the BO/LO/PO for which approval has been granted is not opened within six months from the date of the approval letter, the approval shall lapse. In cases where the non-resident entity is not able to open the office within the stipulated time frame due to reasons beyond its control, the AD Category-I bank may consider granting extension of time for a further period of six months for setting up the office.

question: To which specific official and address must an AD Category-I bank forward an application for opening a BO/LO/PO in India that requires prior approval from the Reserve Bank of India?

question: To which authorities must a Project Office (PO) submit its Annual Activity Certificate (AAC), and how does this differ from the submission requirements for a Liaison Office (LO) or Branch Office (BO)?
answer: A Project Office (PO) must submit its AAC only to its designated AD Category-I bank. In contrast, a Liaison Office (LO) or Branch Office (BO) must submit its AAC to both the designated AD Category-I bank and the Director General of Income Tax (International Taxation), New Delhi.
supporting_quote: The LO/BO needs to submit the AAC to the designated AD Category -I bank as well as Director General of Income Tax (International Taxation), New Delhi whereas the PO needs to submit the AAC only to the designated AD Category -I bank.

question: What are the permitted activities for a liaison office in India of a person resident outside India?

question: When do the Reserve Bank of India (Internal Ombudsman) Directions, 2023 come into effect?

question: What is the specific email address that regulated entities must use to submit the contact details of their appointed Internal Ombudsman to the Reserve Bank of India?
answer: iocepd@rbi.org.in
supporting_quote: The regulated entities are advised to forward the contact details of the Internal Ombudsman / Deputy Internal Ombudsman to Consumer Education and Protection Department, Central Office, Reserve Bank of India, 1st Floor, Amar Building, Sir P M Road, Fort, Mumbai 400 001 (e-mail: iocepd@rbi.org.in) and ensure to update the same as and when there is any change.

question: How does the minimum required years of experience in relevant fields differ between the appointment of an Internal Ombudsman and a Deputy Internal Ombudsman?
answer: An Internal Ombudsman requires a minimum of seven years of experience, whereas a Deputy Internal Ombudsman requires a minimum of five years of experience.
supporting_quote: The Internal Ombudsman shall either be a retired or serving officer, in the rank equivalent to a General Manager of another bank / Financial Sector Regulatory Body / NBSP / NBFC / CIC, having necessary skills and experience of minimum seven years of working in areas such as banking, non-banking finance, regulation, supervision, payment and settlement systems, credit information or consumer protection;... The Deputy Internal Ombudsman shall either be a retired or serving officer, not below the rank of Deputy General Manager of another bank / Financial Sector Regulatory Body / NBSP / NBFC / CIC, having necessary skills and experience of minimum five years of working in areas such as banking, non-banking finance, regulation, supervision, payment and settlement systems, credit information or consumer protection.

question: If a regulated entity newly reaches the prescribed eligibility threshold to fall under these Directions, within what timeframe must it establish an Internal Ombudsman framework, and what is the minimum contractual tenure for the appointed officer?
answer: The entity must establish the framework within six months of reaching the threshold, and the officer must be appointed for a fixed term of not less than three years.
supporting_quote: Any regulated entity, subsequent to the issue of these Directions, reaching the threshold/s prescribed under clause 4(1) shall come under the ambit of these Directions and hence would be required to put in place an Internal Ombudsman framework within six months of reaching the threshold.... The tenure of the Internal Ombudsman / Deputy Internal Ombudsman in the regulated entity shall be a fixed term of not less than three years, but not exceeding five years.

question: Who is defined as the "Competent Authority" for Credit Information Companies under these Directions?

question: How do Commercial Papers (CPs) and Non-Convertible Debentures (NCDs) compare in terms of their minimum allowed tenor and the minimum period required before a buyback can be initiated?
answer: A CP must have a minimum tenor of seven days and can only be bought back after seven days from issuance, whereas an NCD must have a minimum tenor of ninety days and can only be bought back after ninety days from issuance.
supporting_quote: The tenor of a CP shall not be less than seven days or more than one year. The tenor of an NCD shall not be less than ninety days or more than one year. ... question: What are the two conditions that a co-operative society must satisfy regarding its net-worth and its existing fund-based facilities to be eligible to issue Commercial Papers (CPs)?
answer: The co-operative society must have a minimum net-worth of ₹100 crore, and all fund-based facilities it has availed from banks, AIFIs, or NBFCs must be classified as Standard at the time of issue.
supporting_quote: Co-operative societies and limited liability partnerships with a minimum net-worth of ₹100 crore, may also issue CPs under these Directions, subject to the condition that all fund-based facilities availed, if any, by the issuer from banks/ AIFIs / NBFCs are classified as Standard at the time of issue.

question: What is the minimum credit rating required for an issuer to issue Commercial Papers (CPs) and Non-Convertible Debentures (NCDs)?

question: How do the overall overseas investment caps differ between SEBI-registered Mutual Funds (MFs) and Venture Capital Funds (VCFs) or Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs)?

question: What conditions must an Indian entity satisfy before it can make a financial commitment by way of debt to a foreign entity?
answer: The Indian entity must be eligible to make ODI, must have already made ODI in the foreign entity, and must have acquired control in the foreign entity on or before the date of making the financial commitment.
